en: Thus have I heard— *Majjhima Nikāya 109: The Mahāpuṇṇama Sutta* (The Greater Discourse on the Full-Moon Night) Thus have I heard: [One day] the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these four assemblies. Which four? The assembly of nobles, the assembly of brahmins, the assembly of householders, and the assembly of ascetics. These, bhikkhus, are the four assemblies. Of these four assemblies, bhikkhus, the assembly of ascetics is declared by me to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, among all beings—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, many-footed, or having form or formless; whether percipient, non-percipient, or neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient—the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent. Just as, bhikkhus, among all the various kinds of grain, the rice of the finest quality is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent;

even so, bhikkhus, among all beings... the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent. Just as, bhikkhus, among all the various kinds of trees, the sandalwood tree is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent; even so, bhikkhus, among all beings... the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent. Just as, bhikkhus, among all the various kinds of fragrant roots, the root of black orris is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent; even so, bhikkhus, among all beings... the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent. Just as, bhikkhus, among all the various kinds of fragrant heartwoods, the heartwood of red sandalwood is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent; even so, bhikkhus, among all beings... the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent. Just as, bhikkhus, among all the various kinds of fragrant flowers, the jasmine flower is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent; even so, bhikkhus, among all beings... the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent. Just as, bhikkhus, among all the various kinds of fragrant fruits, the mango fruit is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent; even so, bhikkhus, among all beings... the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent. Just as, bhikkhus, among all the various kinds of fragrant scents, the scent of the tagara powder is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent; even so, bhikkhus, among all beings... the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent. Just as, bhikkhus, among all the various kinds of fragrant oils, the oil of jasmine is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent; even so, bhikkhus, among all beings... the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent. Just as, bhikkhus, among all the various kinds of fragrant incenses, the incense of the *sappini* plant is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent; even so, bhikkhus, among all beings... the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent. Just as, bhikkhus, among all the various kinds of fragrant powders, the powder of the *tagara* plant is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent; even so, bhikkhus, among all beings... the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent. Just as, bhikkhus, among all the various kinds of fragrant perfumes, the perfume of the *campaka* flower is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent; even so, bhikkhus, among all beings... the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent. Just as, bhikkhus, among all the various kinds of fragrant substances, the substance of the *punnāga* flower is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent; even so, bhikkhus, among all beings... the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent. Just as, bhikkhus, among all the various kinds of fragrant essences, the essence of the *nāgapuṣpa* flower is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent; even so, bhikkhus, among all beings... the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent. Just as, bhikkhus, among all the various kinds of fragrant waters, the water of the *jātisumana* flower is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent;

even so, bhikkhus, among all beings... the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent. Just as, bhikkhus, among all the various kinds of fragrant garlands, the garland of the *mallikā* jasmine is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent; even so, bhikkhus, among all beings... the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent. Just as, bhikkhus, among all the various kinds of fragrant robes, the robe of fine linen is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent; even so, bhikkhus, among all beings... the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent. Just as, bhikkhus, among all the various kinds of fragrant seats, the seat of the lion is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent; even so, bhikkhus, among all beings... the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is declared to be the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent.
At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, in the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother.
Now on that occasion, on the Uposatha day of the fifteenth, during the full moon night, the Blessed One was seated in the open air surrounded by the community of monks.
Then a certain monk rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, and said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I would ask the Blessed One about a certain point, if the Blessed One would grant me the opportunity for an answer to my question.
“In that case, bhikkhu, sit on your own seat and ask whatever you wish.
Then that bhikkhu, having sat down on his own seat, said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, are these indeed the five aggregates subject to clinging; that is to say:

the form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging?
“Bhikkhu, these are indeed the five aggregates subject to clinging; that is to say:”

“The aggregate of clinging to form, the aggregate of clinging to feeling, the aggregate of clinging to perception, the aggregate of clinging to volitional formations, and the aggregate of clinging to consciousness.
“Excellent, Bhante,” that bhikkhu said, rejoicing and expressing his appreciation for the Blessed One’s words, and he asked the Blessed One a further question:
“But, Bhante, what are these five aggregates of clinging rooted in?”
“Monk, these five aggregates of clinging have desire as their root.
“But, Bhante, is that very clinging the same as those five aggregates of clinging, or is clinging something apart from the five aggregates of clinging?
“Monk, that very clinging is not the same as those five aggregates of clinging, nor is clinging something apart from the five aggregates of clinging.”
“Bhikkhu, whatever desire and lust there is for the five aggregates of clinging—that is the clinging therein.
“But, Bhante, could there be a diversity of desire and lust regarding the five aggregates of clinging?
“There could be, bhikkhu,” the Blessed One said.
“Here, bhikkhu, it occurs to someone: ‘May I be of such form in the future;
may I be of such feeling in the future; may I be of such perception in the future; may I be of such volitional formations in the future; may I be of such consciousness in the future.
In this way, bhikkhu, there is a diversity of desire and lust regarding the five aggregates subject to clinging.”
“But to what extent, venerable sir, is there the designation ‘aggregate’ for the aggregates?
“Bhikkhu, whatever kind of form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all that is the form aggregate.
Whatever kind of feeling there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all that is the feeling aggregate.”
Whatever perception there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—this is the aggregate of perception (*saññā-khandha*).

Whatever mental formations there are—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—this is the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhāra-khandha*).
Whatever consciousness there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—this is the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇa-khandha*).
“To this extent, bhikkhu, there is the designation ‘aggregates’ for the aggregates.
“But what, Bhante, is the cause, what is the condition, for the manifestation of the form aggregate?
What is the cause, what is the condition, for the manifestation of the feeling aggregate?”
“What is the cause, what is the condition for the manifestation of the aggregate of perception?
What is the cause, what is the condition for the manifestation of the aggregate of volitional formations?
What is the cause, what is the condition for the manifestation of the aggregate of consciousness?”
“Bhikkhu, the four great elements are the cause, the four great elements are the condition for the manifestation of the aggregate of form.
Contact is the cause, contact is the condition for the manifestation of the aggregate of feeling.
Contact is the cause, contact is the condition for the manifestation of the aggregate of perception.”
“Contact is the cause, contact is the condition for the manifestation of the aggregate of volitional formations.
Name-and-form, bhikkhu, is the cause, name-and-form is the condition for the manifestation of the aggregate of consciousness.
“But how, venerable sir, does identity view come to be?”

“Here, bhikkhu, an uninstructed worldling—who has no regard for the noble ones, is unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, and undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones; who has no regard for true persons, is unskilled in the Dhamma of true persons, and undisciplined in the Dhamma of true persons—regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as being in self, or self as being in form;
he regards feeling as self, or self as possessing feeling, or feeling as being in self, or self as being in feeling.”
One regards perception as self, or self as possessing perception, or perception as in self, or self as in perception;
one regards volitional formations as self, or self as possessing volitional formations, or volitional formations as in self, or self as in volitional formations;
one regards consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness.
“In this way, bhikkhu, there is identity view.
“But how, Bhante, is there no identity view?

“Here, bhikkhu, the well-taught noble disciple, who has seen the noble ones, is skilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, well-disciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones; who has seen the true persons, is skilled in the Dhamma of the true persons, well-disciplined in the Dhamma of the true persons...”
One does not regard form as self, nor self as possessing form, nor form as in self, nor self as in form;
one does not regard feeling as self, nor self as possessing feeling, nor feeling as in self, nor self as in feeling;
one does not regard perception as self, nor self as possessing perception, nor perception as in self, nor self as in perception.
One does not regard volitional formations as self, nor self as possessing volitional formations, nor volitional formations as being in self, nor self as being in volitional formations;
one does not regard consciousness as self, nor self as possessing consciousness, nor consciousness as being in self, nor self as being in consciousness.
In this way, bhikkhu, personality view does not exist.”
“Venerable sir, what is the gratification in form, what is the danger, and what is the escape?
What is the gratification in feeling, what is the danger, and what is the escape?
What is the gratification in perception, what is the danger, and what is the escape?”
“What is the gratification in volitional formations, what is the danger, and what is the escape?
What is the gratification in consciousness, what is the danger, and what is the escape?
“Bhikkhu, whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on form—that is the gratification in form.”
That form which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in form.
The removal of desire and lust for form, the abandoning of desire and lust for form—this is the escape from form.
Whatever feeling there is, bhikkhu, dependent upon [the body]…
Dependent on perception… dependent on volitional formations… dependent on consciousness,
pleasure and joy arise; this is the gratification in consciousness.
“That consciousness which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in consciousness.
The removal of desire and lust for consciousness, the abandoning of desire and lust for consciousness—this is the escape from consciousness.

“But how, venerable sir, for one who knows what and sees what do the underlying tendencies of ‘I-making,’ ‘mine-making,’ and conceit not arise with regard to this conscious body and all external signs?”
“Bhikkhu, whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle;
inferior or superior; far or near—all form should be seen as it actually is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’”
Whatever feeling there may be … whatever perception there may be … whatever formations there may be …
Whatever consciousness there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle;
inferior or superior; far or near—all consciousness should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self."

“It is for one who knows thus, bhikkhu, and sees thus, that in this body with its consciousness and in all external signs, there are no underlying tendencies of ‘I-making,’ ‘mine-making,’ and conceit.
Then, a certain bhikkhu’s reflection arose in his mind:
“So, it seems, form is not-self, feeling is not-self, perception is not-self, volitional formations are not-self, and consciousness is not-self.”
“...how will actions performed by one who is not-self touch another self?
Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the mind of that bhikkhu, addressed the bhikkhus:
“It is possible, bhikkhus, that some foolish man here, being ignorant and immersed in ignorance, might—his mind dominated by craving—think that he should overstep the Teacher’s instruction:”
‘Thus, sirs, form is not-self, feeling is not-self, perception is not-self, volitional formations are not-self, consciousness is not-self;
how then will actions performed by what is not-self affect a self?
Monks, you have been led away from such views regarding various phenomena.
“What do you think, bhikkhus,
is form permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, Bhante.”
“But is that which is impermanent suffering or happiness?”—
“Suffering, venerable sir.”—
“But is it fitting to regard that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change as:”
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Certainly not, Bhante.
“What do you think, bhikkhus?”
Feeling … perception … volitional formations …
“Is consciousness permanent or impermanent?
“Impermanent, venerable sir.
“But that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”
“It is suffering, venerable sir.
“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus:
‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”
“No, venerable sir.
“Therefore, bhikkhus, whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external;
gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all form [should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom].”
‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’— thus should this be seen as it really is with correct wisdom.
Whatever feeling there is… whatever perception there is…
Whatever formations...
whatever consciousness, whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle;
inferior or superior; far or near—all consciousness is: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self."
‘This is not mine, this is not my self’—thus should it be seen as it really is with correct wisdom.

Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with volitional formations, and disenchanted with consciousness.
Through disenchantment, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
And while this exposition was being spoken, the minds of about sixty bhikkhus were liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
Thus ends the ninth discourse, the Mahāpuṇṇamasutta.
